title: How ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Sets Up a (Hoped for) Third Season
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All November 26, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ethan Hawke in the season two finale of 'The Lowdown.' Shane Brown/FX Logo text [This story contains spoilers for season two of The Lowdown and “The Tower,” the Nov. 25 season finale.] The first season of The Lowdown had a pretty clear resolution : The story that “truthstorian” Lee Raybon ( Ethan Hawke ) had been chasing throughout the season — about the death of the brother (Tim Blake Nelson) of Oklahoma’s likely next governor (Kyle Maclachlan) and their family’s corrupt history — was printed (if not in the form he initially thought) and seemingly put to rest. Season two, however, concludes with multiple threads still untied — and some even circling back to season one. Related Stories TV 'American Horror Story' Finale: Paul Anthony Kelly on the Season 13 Ending: "I Was Flabbergasted" TV 'Snowfall' Spinoff Boss Malcolm Spellman Lays Out Multi-Season Plan for 'The Drop,' Why Season One Was Just a "Dash of What's Coming" Lee, with help from some of the journalists he disparaged at the beginning of the season, gets an exposé on conditions at Judge Sallsman’s (John Hawkes) Fresh Start meatpacking operations published, but he’s frustrated that he can’t tie the judge himself to the story. As he continues chasing leads — including getting Martha Plimpton’s Sheriff Thorne to go on record about the judge — Marty (Keith David) saves Lee from walking into a confrontation with some of the people behind last season’s One Well conspiracy. They realize that Lee’s story about Fresh Start, the One Well people and Marty’s investigation of the illicit sale of indigenous artifacts are all part of a bigger picture. Ginger (Betty Gilpin), meanwhile, leaves Tulsa after realizing that, for several reasons, she can’t continue her life there. In other words, there is a lot left to explore in a potential third season — which FX hasn’t decided on yet. “I’m trying to twist their arm,” The Lowdown creator and showrunner Sterlin Harjo told The Hollywood Reporter about the very open-ended finale. “We left it open and pushed forward to a season three because I like three-season shows. I don’t know if we’re going to be doing it, but I hope that we are.” The finale, titled “The Tower,” did offer closure on one front: Lee, his daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) and their family and friends lay Tommy Lee Jones’ Lee Sr., aka Frog, to rest at a somewhat chaotic funeral, which features the return of Peter Dinklage as Lee’s friend Wendell, who eulogizes Frog with a reading of Dylan Thomas’ “Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night.” That’s followed by a more relaxed, and touching, gathering at Sweet Emily’s afterward, where Francis reads a journal entry of Frog’s detailing the apprehension he felt about being a father when Lee was a baby. “He’s going through the stages of grief. How he understands and reinterprets he and his father’s relationship now that his father’s gone, it’s going to be an ever-changing thing,” Hawke tells THR . “But I feel like something positive and profound happens to Lee when his daughter is reading to him.” Harjo and Hawke talked with THR about the loose plot threads, Lee’s ongoing work of becoming a better person, and how a conversation between Harjo and Jones led to the finale’s prologue. (Separate interviews are combined and edited below.) Before we talk about the end of the season, I want to go back to episode six — where Frog dies at the end of a father-son road trip — because the scenes with Ethan and Tommy are just so, so good. It seems like a huge theme of the season of Lee coming to terms with his dad. He’s kind of starting to get there throughout that episode, but there’s still a lot left for him to process. STERLIN HARJO I would say so. You have this like these two guys that don’t communicate well. I kind of like compare it to the Tim and Dawn love story in the English Office . They have to hide all of their affection, so a touch on the shoulder becomes like a kiss. It’s similar with Lee and Frog because they don’t communicate. These small gestures end up feeling really big. I think them connecting and going home, they don’t say ‘I love you’ or anything like that. But he touches his son on the back. He tells some stories about [Lee’s] mother. All of these things are really big, because they don’t communicate that well, and they have a hard time meeting each other in the middle. I think that that last scene is beautiful where Frog says to Lee, you know, and it almost escapes out of his mouth, “It wasn’t so bad in there, the hospital, and I might have needed a rest.” That’s the apology. Lee is kind of shocked and can’t say anything, and he just nods, which is also his apology and acknowledgement of it. It’s really beautiful moment. And those are my kids that are playing with the bubbles [as Frog watches Lee walk into the convenience store]. I’m really proud of all that. Ryan Kiera Armstrong and Michael Hitchcock Shane Brown/FX ETHAN HAWKE What I like about the writing of the show is it’s never one thing. It’s like more like real life. There is the possibility of healing. It kind of dawns on him at the end of episode six that his father wants to make up with him. And if his father wants to do that, then his father is a different man than he had assumed he was. That opportunity for healing existing is a great benefit to Lee. But of course, they don’t really get to resolve it, and that’s the beauty of episode eight when his daughter is reading from [Frog’s] journal to him. Would the Lee of season one have been able to hand off the Fresh Start story? HAWKE No. Those are the small growths that you get to show in a TV show. What I love about it, having never made a TV show before, the canvas size is just so big that you can really get intimate with a character and show those little adjustments. I don’t think at the beginning of season one that he would have been able to go to his ex-wife’s wedding and not make it about himself. That was a small journey. This journey of showing respect to other journalists was [another]. HARJO It’s such a big deal for me. I wanted that to be a big moment. I opened the season with him calling everyone sellouts and assholes, and then he has to humble himself and go to all of them, hat in hand, and say I need your help. I think it’s also a part of the growth of his personal life and the relationship with his father — him having to realize that he’s not the only one. The story isn’t just about him. There are a lot more loose ends at the end of this season than there were at the end of season one. HARJO We’ve got to twist FX and Disney’s arm for season three. I don’t know how the powers that be work that out. It sure would help if we had awards. Somehow, the Hollywood awards have always been elusive to me and my projects, even though they get reviewed so well. We’ll see what happens, but hopefully something like that happens and that helps us a little bit. I don’t know where we stand right now. I hope to do a season three. Assuming you do go get to go forward — I hope so too — would those loose ends be the primary plot driver in a third season, or more secondary? HARJO It will be the plot of season three, that bigger conspiracy. Obviously there will be some surprises, but what I wanted to do was the idea that season one, you feel like it’s one and done. This is the conspiracy. Then we’re moving on to another conspiracy in season two. One of the things I keep saying in season one is everything’s connected. And actually in Reservation Dogs , we said that a lot too. But the idea is that we were kind of pretending it was going to be these two separate things, but actually they’re all connected. HAWKE The setup is pretty clear. At the end of season two, we see that there’s a connection between the crime of season one and the crime of season two. There’s a connection between this judge and One Well. I think season three would be about bringing the whole tower down. From a character perspective, what do you want to keep exploring with Lee? HAWKE We’ve always kind of dreamed of this as a trilogy. Put simply, season one is about him learning how to be a father, and season two is learning about how to be a son, and a third season would be about him learning to live with himself, and completing the hero’s journey. HARJO I’m really interested in season three being about, What is it like watching your daughter become the next stage of all of that? And also, what does it mean to slow down? What does it mean to look at your life and go, OK, I don’t always have to chase the truth at the detriment of my health, I can also have balance. How do I balance my life, find happiness and find love, and I’m able to be a father and a son and also someone that fights for the truth. How do we become a whole human being and be more responsible? I think that is in the cards for Lee. There weren’t any obvious markers for where Ginger has ended up in her final scene. Where is she as she tries to get away from her former life? HARJO She’s in Eureka Springs [Arkansas], which is a couple hours away from Tulsa going east, and it’s just an interesting old mining and brothel town. It’s really beautiful, in the Ozarks, and a great place to go to get away. We broke off with Betty and took a small group to Eureka Springs and filmed that. I also wanted to ask about the prologue scene in the finale, showing Frog at the fireworks stand in Texas and watching Paris, Texas , which the opening scene of the season pays homage to. Did you just want to give people a sense of where he started this season? HARJO Tommy Lee Jones would call me up now and again. “Hey, I want to talk about the script. You want to come over?” I’d go to his house, and his wife Dawn was awesome, and we would talk about polo or whatever for a little bit. Then he’d say, “All right, come back here,” and we’d go into his office and start talking about the script. At one point, he goes, “Would you like to know where Frog came from?” And I was like, “What do you mean?” He’s like, “Well, the backstory that I came up with.” I was like, “Yeah, of course.” He just told me that story, and I was amazed. It was just the backstory that he had invented — Frog was in Palestine, Texas, working at this fireworks stand. He told me this story, and I was like, “Well, I’ve got to do that. I have to put that in the finale.” So we did. THR

title: India Targets at Least 10 Million AI Workers Through National AI Talent Mission, WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Hears
full_text: × Nov 26, 2026 4:50am PT India Targets at Least 10 Million AI Workers Through National AI Talent Mission, WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Hears By Udita Jhunjhunwala Plus Icon Udita Jhunjhunwala Guest Contributor Latest Vijay Sethupathi’s ‘Maharaja’ Producer Confirms Hollywood Remake Approach as WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Weighs Whether Indian IP Can Travel 1 day ago Women Filmmakers From Kyrgyzstan, Romania and Mexico Push Past Tokenism at IFFI Goa 1 day ago ‘Hanuman Ansh’ Went From Micro-Budget Flop to $48 Million Hit, Director Tells WAVES Film Bazaar 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Uditha Jhunjhunwala India plans to bring at least 10 million people into its AI workforce through the National AI Talent Mission, recently launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, according to Lt. Col. Vikram Singh Bhati, director of the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET). Bhati was speaking at “AI and the Future of Creative Skills: Transforming India’s Media & Entertainment Workforce,” a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar , the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Moderated by voice-over artist and actor Vijay Vikram Singh, the session also featured Amit Meena, director at the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship; K. Satish Nambudiripad, former director general of public broadcaster Doordarshan and chairperson of the Centre for Creative Economy and Public Policy at the National Institute of Technology Calicut; and Biren Ghose, founder and CEO of Astra Studios. Related Stories Chris Pratt to Star in Sci-Fi Family Drama 'The Traveler,' Inks First-Look Producing Deal at Paramount (EXCLUSIVE) Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer' Comeback: A Smaller $5 Million Salary, Optimistic Theater Owners and More “It started with the ministry launching a scheme called SOAR (Skilling for AI Readiness),” Bhati said of the government’s push to prepare workers for AI. He also called on companies to take part, saying “the industry should start absorbing people in the apprenticeship model” to help existing workers and new entrants adapt. AI is changing the production chain, from conceptualization to release, Meena said. “It is democratizing the whole process,” he said, stressing the need to reskill existing workers. Nambudiripad warned that AI tools “tend to homogenize,” and that “India’s folklore, regional languages and cultural nuances could be flattened” if training did not account for the country’s diversity. “You ask five people to write a concept note… if you are going through AI, every one of them will write the same,” he said. He called for technical institutions, film schools and industry to work together, and for skilling to reach India’s smaller tier-two and tier-three cities. Creative skills are shifting “from execution to imagination,” Ghose said, and from software proficiency to technology orchestration. “In the past we were wondering when the tools would catch up with us, and now we’re wondering when we would catch up with the tools,” he said. title: ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Outfit Blueprint & ‘Elsinore’ Producer Lucky Red Team For English-Language Remake Of German Comedy ‘No Hit Wonder’

The original film, which took $3M for Warner Bros Germany last year, features choir-performed versions of Happy by Pharrell Williams and Wrecking Ball by Miley Cyrus. Blueprint is developing and producing the “feel-good tearjerker” with leading Italian indie distributor-producer Lucky Red , which most recently produced Andrew Scott drama Elsinore and Helen Mirren starrer A Talent for Murder as it continues its push into English-language projects. Lucky Red will co-produce the English version, has rights to it in Italy, and may make an Italian version. title: Microdrama Revenues Hit $20B, But Profits Outside China Still Weak – MPA Report
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Denmark’s TV2 Seeks Penance With Acting Program Director Hire After ‘Everyone Loves Rasmus’ Debacle ‘Saint-Pierre’ Season 3 Trailer Sees New Faces Shake Up Life For Fitz & Arch Lauren Ash & Mae Martin Among Cast Of Shozer’s Adult Animation High-School Comedy ‘Dirts’ View All November 25, 2026 7:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Microdrama platform ReelShort Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images The global microdrama business is booming, but outside of China, where ByteDance rules the roost, profits haven’t yet caught up with revenues. That’s according to a Media Partners Asia (MPA) report, which reveals revenues on a global basis are estimated to rise 24% year-on-year to hit $20B in 2026. That will hit $32B by 2031, a growth rate of 9.8% per year, but profitability is still thin. The MPA’s second annual Micro-Drama Economy report notes that outside of China, where microdramas first emerged, every 56 cents in a dollar are spent on marketing and another 18 cents goes to app stores and payment providers, which is significantly reducing earnings. Related Stories News Dogwoof Moves Into Microdrama Game With Tattle TV Deal News Women In Vertical Media: Execs From Shorties Studios, aTwist & Eris Join Inaugural Advisory Circle Excluding China, the microdrama biz is worth $4.87B, with the U.S. the largest at $1.71B, but has fallen 2% year-over-year and will be overtaken by Asia Pacific (excluding China) by 2029. The overall revenue figure will grow to $11B in 2031. Watch on Deadline The MPA noted the two biggest microdrama groups take revenues of more than $1B a year, but within that DramaBox recorded a net margin of 3.2% in 2025 and ReelShort lost $12M, though it made an $8M profit the first quarter of this year. DramaBox and GoodShort , which announced a merger at the end of October, along with ReelShort, Kunlun and NetShort collectively account for 65% of revenues outside of China, where the real action is right now. All four apps are Chinese-owned or backed. India is providing the fastest growth, with revenues tripling this year, as local platforms Kuku TV and Story TV boomed and JioStar debuted in the space in April with JioHotstar service Tadka. India is also the largest Asian market outside China with $322M. MPA’s assessment is that the microdrama business outside of China is not yet settled on a model, but TikTok is predicted to be a dominant force, as it is “positioned on every side” – selling apps’ advertising, carrying their series and, through its free app PineDrama, competing with them. TikTok’s parent, ByteDance is applying the model that shaped the Chinese market – using free, advertising-funded apps to gain audiences first and monetizing later – and MPA predicts it will gain “significant scale in both the U.S.” and Southeast Asia by 2031. Of course, ByteDance was forced to sell a majority of its shares in TikTok in the U.S., but does retain a minority stake. YouTube and Meta are not expected to make a major impression on the microdrama space, while locally the likes of Vigloo in Korea and Fuji TV’s Fod Short in Japan are competing with Chinese-backed apps. China accounts for 76% of total microdrama revenues ($15.2B), following 90% growth in 2025. This will slow to 6.7% in 2031 as viewing plateaus. The MPA doesn’t estimate profits in China as none of the leading players such as top trio ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou single microdrama out in their financial reporting. Advertising on free services took over paid viewing last year, and this year accounts for 69% of revenues, That will grow to 79% in 2031. ByteDance, which operates Hongguo and Douyin, earning 59% of China’s revenues. ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou collectively account for 82% of the market. MPA calculates revenue as what viewers, advertisers and brands pay before app-store and payment fees; and outside China it covers dedicated apps and their web stores, not general social feeds. In China, MPA’s estimates exclude producers’ spending on AI models and platform investment, which are both included in the National Radio and Television Administration’s RMB100B estimate for 2025. “Demand for micro drama is established in every major market, but outside China this is still an emerging business, and it has yet to show that it can earn a durable profit,” said Vivek Couto, CEO and Executive Director of MPA. “The leading apps spend more than half of their revenue to acquire viewers, and most of those viewers do not pay. Consolidation has begun, and China has already moved to free, advertising-funded viewing. The companies that endure will be those that retain their viewers, bill them directly and invest in titles worth returning to.” The MPA report raised a further notable asides: new title listings on apps outside China rose from about 100,000 in 2025 to 440,000 in 2026, and 75% were made with AI. This counts series that are made in different languages more than once. MPA’s research shows an AI-made title costs “about a tenth of a series filmed in Los Angeles,” it added. “AI has made a title cheap enough to test almost any idea, and catalogues have filled accordingly,” said Myat Pan Phyu (May), Lead Analyst, Micro Drama and Vertical Video for MPA. “Viewing has moved far less: live action still dominates the leading titles on most of the platforms we track. “What decides a platform’s economics is how many of its titles earn back the marketing spent on them. That favours companies with established IP, stars and audiences of their own, which is why local broadcasters, studios and telecom operators matter to the next phase.” ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Firing Up Thanksgiving With $85M+ Five-Day Haul Judge Sides With ABC In First Amendment Lawsuit Against FCC U2 Delivers Halftime Goods During NFL’s First Thanksgiving Eve Game Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed Due To Weather; NBC To Air 2025 Event Read More About: 2 Comments

title: Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL’s First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL’s First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton Andy Taylor Dies: Duran Duran Guitarist Was 65 Done Deal! Netflix Buys Radford Studios For Almost $400M; Streamer Calls Purchase “A Meaningful New Investment In California’s Film Industry” View All November 25, 2026 7:06pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bono set to perform with U2 at 2026 Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show on Netflix Getty Images / NFL / Netflix No matter how many hits and tricks U2 pulled out of the hat at L.A.’s SoFi Stadium , today’s Bono Bowl on Netflix was always going to live in the shadow of the streamer’s square dancing filled Beyoncé Bowl from Christmas Day 2024 . Accepting the inevitable, the elder statesmen of anthem rock took their halftime spin on stage at the NFL ’s first ever Thanksgiving Eve game to go full bread and circuses. Giving the people and the streamer what they wanted, the nine-minute show wasn’t as dramatic as the currently 13-13 match-up between the hometown L.A. Rams and the Green Bay Packers , but it didn’t have to be. All U2 had to do tonight was show everyone they still have gas in the tank. Under those criteria, in their first time headlining on Netflix, the Irish rockers succeeded. Related Stories Sports NFL On The Future Of Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve Game & Starting A New Tradition: “We Are Committed” News U2 Sets North American Stops On 2027 Stadium Tour; 2 LA Shows Planned Veering towards the tried and true, Bono, guitarist The Edge, bassiest Adam Clayton and drummer Larry Mullen Jr thundered through their Boomer classics of “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” The Joshua Tree ’s “Where The Streets Have No Name” and MLK tribute “Pride (In The Name of Love).” Add to that a sprinkle of The Supremes “Stop! In the Name of Love” via some glorious vocals thrown in from teh Grammy nominated Womack Sisters and the beats of an on-field marching band and you have an All-American party — which is precisely what a NFL halftime show is supposed to be. U2 performs 'Where The Streets Have No Name' at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve halftime show. pic.twitter.com/dXhj4KQbPk — Netflix (@netflix) November 26, 2026 In a nod to their latest release and the times we live in, the second song in the set poignantly was the “Torn” duet with Dolly Parton Dolly Forever <3 U2 pays tribute to Dolly Parton with “Torn” during their halftime performance pic.twitter.com/c4CfeoQiXi — Netflix (@netflix) November 26, 2026 With the obvious exception of the inclusion of the late great Dolly, who was displayed on flowing curtains that came down from the stadium roof, it was a set that could have come almost anytime the last 40 years. In fact, besides “Torn” (Parton’s last recording), every song in U2’s Thanksgiving Eve set came from when Ronald Reagan was President. Bono’s vow not to use backing tracks and the pre-halftime shot that Netflix showed of U2 heading through Sofi’s catacombs on gold carts sorta told you all you needed to know. To their credit, unlike most Super Bowl halftime shows of the past dozen years, (and expected for Jay-Z’s Super Bowl LXI set on February 14 at Sofi), a relatively stripped down U2 didn’t bring on any super star guests for the L.A. crowd. Walking out on the field to a chorus, the usually-chatty band took the in-the-round stage with a “thank you for having us” and said little more. (L-R) The Edge, Bono, Larry Mullen Jr. and Adam Clayton of U2 perform onstage at SoFi Stadium on Nov 25, 2026 in Inglewood, CA Oddly ending a bit too quickly, tonight’s shindig came halfway through the NFL’s first Thanksgiving Eve match with the Rams battling it out with Packers at the L.A. team’s camera-ready stadium. A clear belt notch in the league’s desire to dramatically expand the incredibly lucrative football franchise, tonight’s much-hyped game between the Packers and the Rams was given all the gloss of a playoff clash or the Super Bowl itself by the Ted Sarandos and Greg Peter-run streamer. Having already played a few warm-up gigs — like opening the November 14 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame ceremony — during the extensive promotional tour this month for their recently released Carnaval De Luz album, tonight gave U2 a further chance to reach fans old and new. Aided by a stage that was rolled out and set up in less than 8 minutes, a 52-foot telescopic camera crane and a specialty camera coming down from the Sofi roof, the Jesse Collins Entertainment-produced set had a very professional shine. WHAT A PERFORMANCE U2 performs '(Pride) In The Name of Love' with The Womack Sisters at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show pic.twitter.com/ZBzEZ1SUIt — Netflix (@netflix) November 26, 2026 For a soaring-gesture band never shy of taking big stages in a big way, the global reach can only help U2 hawk a few more tickets for their upcoming Greatest Show on Earth tour . The tour begins in Mexico City in February. After shows in South America and Europe, the band and their unofficial 50 th anniversary tour ends up in North America for a 15-stadium run starting in Miami on August 13. At the same time, as the Rolling Stones, Bruce Springsteen and many other stadium-playing legacy acts will tell you, the role of old bands is to play the old hits — no matter how good or bad the latest album is. Bono, the Edge, Mullen and Clayton knew that back in 2002 when they played Super Bowl XXXVI in the aftermath of the 9/11 terror attacks. Using their Elevation Tour set at NOLA’s Superdome, U2 in less than 20-minutes whipped off “Beautiful Day,” “MLK” and “Where The Streets Have No Name” and paid tribute via curtain with the names of the fallen on it to those who lost their lives that horrible day in NYC. One of the biggest bands in the world for 40 years, U2 haven’t toured since 2019, and they had a bit to prove tonight, as they made clear. Yet, the GameDay halftime show wasn’t their first time on stage this decade. A 40-show stint at Vegas’ Sphere starting in September 2023 saw the band pulling it off Zoo TV style, even with an injured Mullen sitting it out. Still, a big live draw since the mid-1980s no matter how their records charted, the Irving and Jeffrey Azoff-managed U2 are leaving no opportunity unexplored this year in a hope to return to relevance. Even Sofi itself got in on the act on Wednesday. Tickets on sale on December 4 on Ticketmaster 🎟️ pic.twitter.com/KnB9CkgIQp — SoFi Stadium (@SoFiStadium) November 25, 2026 With ads galore and L.A. beauty shots tonight, Netflix has finally worked out most of the kinks that marred some of their past live sports events. Fueled by play-by-play from Noah Eagle and analysis from Hall-of-Famer Luke Kuechly, the primetime result so far delivered a slick and seamless product that moved at the pace of the action on the field. Simply put (and hear me Jeff Bezos), Netflix equaled what ESPN and Monday Night Football have been doing for ages — which is no small feat when you consider that the streamer’s initial live sporting event was just over three years ago with the mash-up golf tournament The Netflix Cup. From the big picture perspective, tonight’s game and that halftime show can’t but help Netflix’s ongoing bid to FIFA for the 2030 World Cup. Netflix ’s animated adventure film Steps , co-directed with John Ripa , casts Lilith ( Ali Wong ) and Margot ( Stephanie Hsu ) as Asian immigrants in a French-inspired fairytale kingdom, where questions of belonging and privilege shape their search for happiness. Meanwhile, Cinderella ( Amanda Seyfried ) must also learn to confront her own societal complacency and dismantle stereotypes that her inherently kind nature unintentionally upholds. Here with Deadline, Tzue discusses the film’s unique visual style, reworking a traditional fairytale and bringing in new “punk rock” dimensions. Watch on Deadline ALYCE TZUE: It began when Riki Lindhome and Kate Micucci had the idea for the stepsisters’ perspective and pitched it to Amy Poehler’s company, Paper Kite, which then brought it to Netflix. When I came on board, I made the stepsisters Asian immigrants to a fairytale world. We started with these pillars and bigger concepts that we wanted to honor. One was these outsider sisters who don’t fit into the box of what you would traditionally see as a protagonist getting their happily-ever-after. That does involve race, but also the traditional feminine archetype that’s super soft-spoken and polite, sings to animals, is pretty, and has that face shape you see in every animated movie. We wanted them to find their unique happily-ever-after. There was another idea where we wanted to speak about magic as privilege. Of course, Cinderella has gone through a lot of hardship, but you can also ask, “Well, other people in this world have gone through hardship, too. Why is it this one girl who’s elevated above everyone else and has a fairy godmother, a magic dress and all of that?” That was another concept we wanted to speak to.

title: Baz Bamigboye Pays Tribute To Legendary British Agent Jeremy Conway – With Help From Helena Bonham Carter
full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz Breaking Baz: ‘Bunker’ Writer-Director Florian Zeller Takes Us Behind The Scenes With Penélope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Stephen Graham & Dame Eileen Atkins Robert Pattinson As James Bond? Baz Bamigboye Has Some Thoughts Renate Reinsve On Making Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Winner ‘Fjord’: “I Knew I Was Going Into A Completely Different World” View All November 26, 2026 2:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jeremy Conway, seated centre, with his colleagues. Courtesy CVGG. Jeremy Conway — an artiste’s agent, and a titan of the industry with an unerring eye for the stars of the future — died earlier this month aged 87. His client list was legendary, a rollcall that included Anthony Hopkins , Brian Cox, Helena Bonham Carter , Benedict Cumberbatch, Claire Bloom, Greta Scacchi, Noma Dumezweni, Joanne Froggatt, and David Harewood,. Over 50 years ago, Conway founded his eponymous agency. In 1980, Nicki Van Gelder joined him, adding her name to the shingle. There were just three of them in the office then, and when John Grant joined in 1994 there were nine. “We are now 32!” Grant recently told Deadline of the company that’s now a powerhouse called Conway Van Gelder Grant . Grant confirmed that Conway — “his friend and mentor” — had died on 1 November this year. Conway was CVGG’s principal partner until he retired in 2015. Related Stories News Breaking Baz: 'Bunker' Writer-Director Florian Zeller Takes Us Behind The Scenes With Penélope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Stephen Graham & Dame Eileen Atkins News Anthony Hopkins To Star In Post-Apocalyptic Sci-Fi '2048' -- TIFF Market In a tribute penned for Deadline, Bonham Carter, who’s still with the agency, recalled a note she had written for Conway’s retirement party thanking him “for my career.” She meant it. She continued, “I don’t think any of it would have happened if it weren’t for him. He started it all; 42 years ago, I was 17 and sitting in Jeremy’s office on a rather low futon or sofa watching him pace up and down in front of me in mild frustration. He had seen me in a Channel 4 drama playing an Edwardian ghost [1983’s A Pattern of Roses ] and was convinced I had something. I wasn’t so sure. I thought I should go to university. ‘Look,’ he said somewhat impatiently. ‘I really am one of the top five agents in London.’ And so began one of my longest partnerships in my life. We did, I think about 20 years together. And I never did go to university. And nor did I ever train.” Watch on Deadline Conway wasted no time. He fired off a message to Trevor Nunn suggesting that he consider Bonham Carter for the title role in Lady Jane , Nunn’s film about Lady Jane Grey, the 16 th -century “Nine Days Queen”. Next, Conway took Celestia Fox, Merchant Ivory’s casting director for a jolly supper, where he advocated Bonham Carter for the role of Lucy Honeychurch in their upcoming production of A Room with a View . During this period, Grant remarked, “Jeremy represented several of each cast of the Merchant Ivory Films.” Anthony Hopkins and Bonham Carter both starred in Howard’s End , while Hopkins went on to make Remains of the Day . Cross-referencing the Merchant Ivory catalogue, it’s possible to discern that, over a period of three decades, scores of CVGG artistes populated their films. I met Conway many times over the years — at first nights, at Oscar-night soirées in Hollywood — and every now and then we’d have lunch. He once explained that, as the son of Colonel Charles Maxwell Orr Sawers, a colonel in the 9th Royal Deccan Horse who served in India and Burma, he knew all about “getting work done and just getting on with it.” I found that comment from Conway in a red Silvine notebook, one of hundreds that I forgot to throw away. The army-brat background, I think, gave Conway that carpe diem attitude, but it was cloaked by his avuncular bearing. But he was definitely getting on with it when he got his hands on Ted Tally’s screenplay for The Silence of the Lambs . And he was getting stuff done when suggested that the film’s director Jonathan Demme go and watch Hopkins in David Hare and Howard Brenton’s play Pravda , which opened at London’s National Theatre in May 1985. The part of Hannibal Lecter won Hopkins his first Academy Award. Conway loved actors. I would often catch him at plays well into their runs, featuring thespians that he didn’t represent. He wasn’t out to poach them; he just wanted to watch great performances. Jeremy Conway’s Spotlight page Born David Maxwell Sawers, Conway attended Radley College in Abingdon, in Oxford. After that, he studied drama at the Guildhall School of Music & Drama., which is where he met his life-long partner Neville Phillips, with whom he entered into a civil partnership in 2005. Parts in Z Cars , early episodes of Doctor Who and stage roles followed, but Conway enjoyed watching the likes of Judi Dench, Maggie Smith and Hopkins at the Old Vic rather more than treading the boards himself. Deciding to become an agent, he joined forces with former Royal Academy of Dramatic Arts-trained actor-turned-agent Norman Boyack. Together they formed Boyack and Conway, where their roster included John Thaw, Sheila Hancock and Edward Hardwicke. When Boyack decided to leave the business, Conway set up on his own, representing Hopkins, Susan Penhaligon and Trudie Styler, then an actress, early on in her career. Once Van Gelder joined, the business grew. Grant observed that Conway was “definitely one of the first agents in London to represent European and world film actors from various countries. As wide a range as Romania, Scandinavia, Germany, France and India. Notably Jesper Christensen, Lars Mikkelsen — who’s still with us — and Om Puri.” Aside from his film, theatre and television passions, Conway loved to cook and entertain, and he would regularly host dinner parties at the weekend, inviting the good and the great of the entertainment world. Grant added that he was a keen gardener and collector of art and artefacts. “He was also an avid reader,” Grant marveled, “and somehow found time to read many books alongside a large volume of scripts. He had an encyclopedic knowledge of plays and could frequently be heard discussing why someone was specifically right for a role.” For over a decade Conway was a board director of the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, where he was first in line to scoop up tomorrow’s stars. He was also long associated with Bafta, having been a member for 60 years. A better-than-thriving CVGG is Conway’s legacy; he always had one eye on the future by partnering with Van Gelder and Grant. How he went to bat for all his actors mattered most. I remember being on the set of Guy Ritchie and Matthew Vaughn’s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels when Jason Flemyng inched his way over to me for a chat and he was almost in tears as he told how Conway had saved his life by “giving me a career”. That’s precisely the side of Conway’s character that Bonham Carter reflected on in her tribute to her beloved agent, which I’m posting in full below… “I think for Jeremy’s retirement party I wrote a note saying, ‘Thank you for my career.’ I meant it. I don’t think any of it would have happened if it weren’t for him. He started it all; 42 years ago, I was 17 and sitting in Jeremy’s office on a rather low futon or sofa watching him pace up and down in front of me in mild frustration. He had seen me in a Channel 4 drama playing an Edwardian ghost and was convinced I had something. I wasn’t so sure. I thought I should go to university. ‘Look,’ he said somewhat impatiently. ‘I really am one of the top five agents in London.’ And so began one of my longest partnerships in my life. We did, I think about 20 years together. And I never did go to university. And nor did I ever train. “Jeremy was my industry parent. He was my champion. And patron. My enthusiast. He was bossy, impatient, and had formidable energy and appetite for all things life had to offer. He had great taste. His house, when I last saw him, was brimful of paintings and objects of beauty. He loved his job and he loved it for the culture of it — the plays, the acting, the life, art, the people. His interest and curiosity was acute. “Of course, most of our relationship was conducted on the phone. He had a great, handsome, fully resonant telephone voice. He had trained as an actor and would always intone, ‘CON-sonants, Helly!’ “One of my favorite poets, Mary Oliver, ends one of her poems, by saying, ‘I don’t want to end up having simply visited this world.’ Jeremy didn’t just visit it, he ate it, and he tasted it. He explored, and he made people’s careers and opened doors, and he grew an agency from seed that lives and thrives. “His legacy and his children are the agency and all those he impacted, people whose lives would be utterly different without him. His family of connections and tentacles of influence over decades in the industry is like a tree with many roots, an old oak that will far outlive us all. “I think of him with huge love and gratitude. I was all his idea. title: Richard Hammond Says He Was Approached By BBC About ‘Top Gear’ Return
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Richard Hammond Says He Was Approached By BBC About ‘Top Gear’ Return BBC Journalists Vote To Take Strike Action Over Job Cuts ‘I’m A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here!’ Row Over “Microaggressions” Sparks 900 Complaints View All November 26, 2026 2:52am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Richard Hammond BBC Richard Hammond has revealed that the BBC sounded him out about getting back behind the Top Gear wheel for the show’s upcoming reboot. The presenter said he declined the opportunity to return to the motoring show he helped turn into a global phenomenon alongside Jeremy Clarkson and James May . Hammond disclosed the BBC’s approach during an interview with Times Radio on the day that Gordon Ramsay was unveiled as the new host of Top Gear. “I did talk to them about Top Gear relaunching, and I’m sure they went to the others as well. They came to me, and [asked] was I interested? ‘No, I’m too old,’ [I responded],” Hammond said. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Gordon Ramsay To Host Revived 'Top Gear' For BBC News BBC Journalists Vote To Take Strike Action Over Job Cuts “I’ve done it. I wouldn’t want to revisit it. That was our Top Gear , wasn’t it? We did it, the three of us, and when we left and went on together, it was the three of us. But that was our show. “The BBC owns Top Gear and has had it for decades, and I think right now should be making a show that actually tells us what’s happening in the world of cars.” Times Radio presenter Kait Borsay asked Hammond if he would be interested if Clarkson and May returned to Top Gear. “We’ve done it. Let somebody else. We made our show in the way we did, and for our time,” he replied. “The BBC should be making a TV show that tells us, the consumers: This is what’s happening in the world of transport.” Hammond hosted Top Gear between 2002 and 2015, before leaving the BBC with Clarkson and May and launching The Grand Tour on Amazon Prime Video. Ramsay was announced as the next host of Top Gear four years after Andrew Flintoff’s crash. Ramsay will lead the series alongside a soon-to-be-announced lineup of co-presenters, with The Stig returning. Filming will take place across the UK and around the world in 2027, with the Top Gear test track at Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey once again serving as the show’s home. Ramsay said: “At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected – surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos. title: Huw Edwards To Speak On TV For First Time About Criminal Actions & Fall From Grace In Channel 4 Doc
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Netflix Posts Racy Thanksgiving Message On ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 2 Premiere Day BBC Being Investigated Over Antisemitism By Government Adviser Huw Edwards To Speak On TV For First Time About Criminal Actions & Fall From Grace In Channel 4 Doc View All November 26, 2026 3:11am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Huw Edwards Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu via Getty Images “From trusted national figure to registered sex offender,” Huw Edwards is to be interviewed and profiled in a Channel 4 documentary next week. Huw Edwards – Guilty will see the disgraced newsreader face questions publicly for the first time on TV about his criminal actions and astonishing fall from grace. Airing Tuesday at 9 p.m. GMT (1 p.m. PT), the documentary follows the ex- BBC News anchor at his home in rural Wales as he navigates his existence in the wake of grooming allegations and his conviction of making indecent images of children. Related Stories News Richard Hammond Says He Was Approached By BBC About 'Top Gear' Return News Gordon Ramsay To Host Revived 'Top Gear' For BBC A short trailer sees Edwards say “I’d lost the plot” after being questioned over why he did what he did. The interviewer can then be heard saying exasperatedly, “Oh, come on.” Watch on Deadline Channel 4 described the doc as “an uncomfortable portrayal of what happens when a previously beloved public figure betrays the trust of the people and asks what accountability really means in the wake of a serious criminal conviction?” We understand Edwards was not paid to take part in the documentary and had no editorial control. He has addressed his actions on his Substack but this will be the first time he speaks about them on TV with an interviewer. Edwards rose to become one of the UK’s best-known news anchors before workplace misconduct allegations and a child pornography conviction ruined his reputation. In 2024, he pled guilty to making indecent images of children and was given a suspended sentence. A Martin Clunes-starring 5 drama about him, Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards , is currently being probed by regulator Ofcom over “fairness and privacy.” Sacha Mirzoeff, Senior Commissioning Editor at Channel 4, said: “Channel 4 has an established reputation for tackling controversial subjects through exemplary filmmaking. Huw Edwards – Guilty is no exception in its quest for answers from a man who is trying to come to terms with his abuse of power.” Director Patrick Forbes added: “This was an important film to make. It’s rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues – whether it’s celebrity culture or the power of the media – as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment.” Huw Edwards – Guilty is commissioned by Mirzoeff and produced by Oxford Films . The producer is Stephanie Collins.
